deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is part of a German lecture or study notebook on ancient history, specifically the Persian empire. It continues the account of Cyrus from the previous page and leads into Cambyses and Darius on the next. The neat, regular German Kurrent is probably not Gauss's own mathematical hand; it may be student or lecture notes bound into the bundle.

Content of the page, in order:
(1) The Persians adopted the Median religion, i.e. the Magian religion, which the note says still prevails in parts of Asia. Its founder was Zoroaster, who appeared as a reformer in Media.
(2) Cyrus died in 529 BC and left two sons, Cambyses and Smerdis. He divided the empire between them: Cambyses received the western part and Smerdis the eastern, but Cambyses was to be overlord of all the lands.
(3) Dissatisfied, Cambyses had his younger brother killed. He then turned conqueror in Africa.
(4) Egypt was ruled by Amasis. Amasis died and was succeeded by Psammenit (Psammetichus III). A single main battle and the capture of Memphis made Cambyses master of Egypt.
(5) Cambyses then wanted to subdue the rest of Africa. Three expeditions were planned from Egypt: against Carthage, against the temple and oracle of Jupiter Ammon, and against Ethiopia.
(6) The campaign against Carthage did not happen 'because they had no fleet'. The other two were sent out, a sentence that continues on the next page.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct. The only numbers are dates (529 a.C.) and the count of '2 sons' and '3 expeditions'. The surrounding pages give 529–522 for Cambyses and 522–486 (36 years) for Darius I.
errors: Not mathematical errors but historical inaccuracies relative to modern scholarship.
Cyrus's death is now usually dated 530 BC, not 529 BC; 529 follows an older chronology.
Herodotus (III.19) says the Carthage expedition failed because the Phoenician fleet refused to sail against their own colony, not because the Persians had no fleet at all.
Treating Zoroaster as the founder of the 'Magian' religion, and as a reformer specifically in Media, reflects 18th/early-19th-century views.
The page's statement that Cyrus divided the empire between his sons follows Ctesias and Xenophon-type traditions, not Herodotus.

results.what: Lecture notes on Achaemenid Persian history: Zoroastrian/Magian religion, the succession from Cyrus to Cambyses and Smerdis, Cambyses' conquest of Egypt (Amasis, Psammenit, Memphis), and his planned expeditions to Carthage, Ammon and Ethiopia
results.usually_credited_to: Herodotus, Histories Book III (ancient source); standard early-19th-century school/university history curriculum

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical lecture or study notes on Persian history with no mathematical content. It is likely not even in Gauss's hand. Nothing here bears on Gauss's mathematics.

checkable.asserts: The reign of Cambyses as dated on the adjacent page (529–522 BC) lasts 7 years.
The reign of Darius I as dated on the next page (522–486 BC) matches the stated 36 years.

transcription_corrections: Line 'Gegen Karthago, dem Tempel und Orakel': the dative 'dem' is what the manuscript shows; read in context as 'gegen ... den Tempel'.
The final word 'beid.' is an abbreviation of 'beiden', continuing on the next page ('... die andern beiden [ausgerüstet] und geschickt').
The first word 'versetzen' may be 'versetzten' (past tense); the hand is ambiguous.
